content.text: No minimum commitment or take-or-pay exists. The fee structure is license fees, annual maintenance/access fees, and revenue share tied to actual customer revenue — with unlimited users and no volume caps on us.

input.quote: 2. Corio Customer Application Management Revenue: Corio to pay Commerce One [*] of all Application Management Revenue from Corio Customers for use of Commerce One Software or MarketSite.net Service Access subject to the following limitations.
input.rationale:
This meets the preferred position: the agreement imposes no minimum purchase commitment, take-or-pay obligation, or volume commitment on Corio. Our payment obligations are limited to (i) the one-time BuySite license fee due on Software Acceptance, (ii) annual maintenance/support and MarketSite.net access fees for services actually made available, and (iii) a revenue share calculated on actual Application Management Revenue received from Corio Customers — i.e., pure pass-through of realized usage, with no floor, no guaranteed minimum, and no shortfall penalty. Exhibit B expressly sets Software Users at "Unlimited," so there is no volume cap on our usage either.

Three points noted but not flagged. First, the "minimum limitation of 40 Authorized Software Users per Customer" in Exhibit B (p0158) is a qualifying threshold on the revenue-share *exemption* for the initial 3000 licenses, not a purchase commitment or seat minimum we must buy or pay for. Second, the five-year initial term (Section 11.1) with no termination-for-convenience right is a term-length point rather than a minimum-volume commitment, and Section 4.2 makes maintenance continuation expressly conditional on Corio electing to "continue to pay" the annual fees, which gives us a practical exit from the recurring spend. Third, Exhibit D's sales and marketing items — including the two-customer order target — are stated as "non-binding" and qualified by "commercially reasonable efforts," so they create no enforceable volume obligation. The shortfall reference in Section 4.4 concerns audit true-up of amounts payable and is mutual ("the appropriate party shall promptly pay the amount of such shortfall or refund such overpayment"), which is the true-up mechanic the playbook prefers rather than a penalty. No redline required.
